concepts.title: Protein in everyday food
concepts.hook: Dal, milk, eggs and nuts all carry protein, and dal with rice fills gaps that each food has alone.
concepts.rule: Milk, eggs, fish, meat, pulses and nuts carry protein. Cereals and pulses fill each other's gaps. Healthy adults need about 0.83 g per kg of body weight a day; teens, pregnant women and the ill need more.

claims.text: Milk, meat, fish, eggs and pulses are rich sources of protein, and nuts and seeds also hold a good amount.
Cereals or millets and pulses can fill gaps in each other’s amino acid mix.
The body uses 20 amino acids to build proteins. Nine of them cannot be made in the body, so they come from food, and animal foods carry all nine.
India's food guide sets a daily protein allowance of 0.83 g per kg of body weight for healthy adults, about 54 g for a 65 kg adult.
India's food guide says cereals and pulses in a 3 to 1 ratio by raw weight meet the need for all essential amino acids.
Growing children and teens, pregnant women and people who are ill or under physical stress need more protein. Sports guidance gives people who exercise 1.4 to 2.0 g per kg a day.
Nuts and oilseeds are rich in fat, while pulses are low in fat and high in fibre.

items.stem: A gym friend says you cannot get enough protein without eating meat. What is not quite right?

options.text: Pulses, milk, nuts and seeds carry protein too.
options.feedback: India's food guide lists pulses, milk, nuts and seeds as protein sources, so meat is one choice among many.

options.text: No; meat is the one real source.
options.feedback: Meat is one source, but pulses, milk, nuts and seeds are good protein foods as well.

options.text: Plants have protein, but rice has the most of all.
options.feedback: Rice is not one of the rich protein foods. Pulses, milk, nuts and seeds are.

items.stem: Deepak swaps his daily dal for a big bowl of nuts to get more protein. What is the catch?

options.text: Nuts bring a lot of fat with their protein.
options.feedback: Nuts and seeds do carry protein, but they are also rich in fat. Pulses like dal are low in fat.

options.text: Nuts hold no protein of any kind.
options.feedback: Nuts do carry a fair amount of protein. The catch is the fat that comes with it.

options.text: Dal has more fat in it than a bowl of nuts.
options.feedback: It is the other way round. Pulses are low-fat foods, while nuts are rich in fat.

options.feedback: Pulses run short of a building block that cereals have plenty of, so rice or roti fills it.

options.feedback: Chana is another pulse with the same gap, so it cannot fill what rajma lacks.

options.feedback: Eggs carry all nine building blocks, but aloo is not on the protein list, so that thali needs dal.
Eggs already carry all nine building blocks, so the egg thali covers the roti's gap.

options.text: Both of them need a pulse added.
options.feedback: The egg thali is covered, since eggs bring all nine blocks. The aloo thali is the one that needs dal.

items.stem: A hostel cook plans the day's protein for ten adults from the healthy-adult figure per kg. Two of them are pregnant. Why is that plan incomplete?

options.text: Pregnant women need more than that figure.
options.feedback: Right. The per-kg figure is for healthy adults. Pregnant women need more, so their share of the menu has to grow.

options.text: Pregnant women need less protein than others.
options.feedback: It runs the other way. Pregnancy raises the need above the healthy-adult figure.

options.text: No; the figure fits each adult alike.
options.feedback: The figure fits healthy adults. Teens, pregnant women and people who are ill need more than it gives.

items.stem: About how many grams of protein per kg of body weight does a healthy adult need each day?

options.feedback: Right. India's food guide sets about 0.83 g per kg a day for healthy adults. Teens, pregnant women and athletes may need more.
That is far above the figure. Healthy adults need about 0.83 g per kg a day.
That is far too low. The guide's figure for healthy adults is about 0.83 g per kg a day.

steps.title: Where protein comes from

steps.title: Cereal and pulse fill each other's gaps

concepts.title: Free sugars
concepts.hook: The sugar in fruit juice counts as free sugar, even when no spoonful of sugar was added.
concepts.rule: Free sugars include added sugar, jaggery, honey, syrups and fruit juice sugars. On a 2,000 kcal day, under 10% of energy is about 50 g; less may add benefit. Drinks and sauces hide a lot.

claims.text: WHO counts added sugar and the sugars in honey, syrups and fruit juice as free sugars, but not the sugars in whole fresh fruit, vegetables or milk, since no harm from those has been reported.
WHO says free sugars should give less than 10% of daily energy, because more raises the risk of overweight, obesity and tooth decay. At 5% or less, there may be more benefit.
On a 2,000 kcal day, 10% of energy from free sugars is about 50 g, or about 12 level teaspoons.
One can of sugar-sweetened soda can hold up to 40 g of free sugars, about 10 teaspoons, and a tablespoon of ketchup about 4 g.
India's food guide says sugar should give less than 5% of daily energy for adults, and counts jaggery and honey as sugars.

options.text: Neither, since no sugar was added.

options.text: the warm water turns it into a syrup

options.text: it was bought in a shop

concepts.title: Hydration cues
concepts.hook: Tea and milk count as fluid, about 2 litres a day is a rough guide, and pee colour is a simple daily cue.
concepts.rule: Water, milk and lower-sugar tea or coffee all add fluid; about 2 litres a day is a rough guide. Pale yellow pee is the aim. Heat and hard activity raise needs, and some signs need urgent help.

claims.text: India's food guide says a healthy person needs about eight glasses, or 2 litres, of water a day, other drinks included. The body loses water through sweat, pee and stool.
Water, lower-fat milk and lower-sugar drinks, including tea and coffee, all count towards daily fluid.
Most people can aim for pee that is a clear pale yellow; thirst, a dry mouth, tiredness, dark yellow pee and peeing less often are signs of low fluid.
Fluid needs rise in very hot weather and during hard or long activity, because the body loses a lot of water through sweat.
On hot days, India's food guide likes buttermilk, coconut water or lemon water. But it says those with some kidney or heart problems should not drink coconut water.
Dizziness on standing that does not go away, confusion, or far less pee than normal can be signs of serious dehydration. These need urgent help.

options.text: It is a rough guide, and other drinks count.

options.text: Nothing; 8 glasses of plain water is the rule.

That would be 20 litres. 2,000 ml divided by 200 ml is 10 tumblers.

items.stem: On a long train journey, Sudeep drinks very little so he can skip the toilet. By evening, what will his pee likely show?

options.text: Dark yellow, a sign he is low on fluid.
options.feedback: Drinking little with no top-up leaves the body short, and dark yellow pee is the sign.

options.text: Pale yellow, since sitting saves water.
options.feedback: Sitting still does not stop water loss. With little to drink, pee turns dark.

options.text: No change from a normal day.
options.feedback: Taking in less fluid shows up in pee colour, which turns darker.

items.stem: Faria drinks about eight cups of tea a day and little plain water, and her pee is pale yellow. Is she short of fluid?

options.text: No; tea counts, and pale pee shows enough.
options.feedback: Lower-sugar tea counts as fluid, and pale yellow pee is the sign of drinking enough.

options.text: Yes; tea does not count as fluid.
options.feedback: Tea does count as fluid. Her pale pee also shows she is drinking enough.

options.text: Yes; pale pee means she is short of water.
options.feedback: Pale yellow is the aim. Dark yellow pee would be the sign of low fluid.

items.stem: Dadaji has heart trouble, and his doctor told him to limit fluids. In the monsoon heat, his grandson urges him to drink extra. What is the safer step?

options.feedback: A limit set by his doctor comes first, even on hot days, because his heart condition changes what is safe.

options.text: Drink double, since heat raises everyone's need.
options.feedback: Heat raises the need for most people, but a doctor's fluid limit is set for his heart, so it comes first.

options.text: Switch to plenty of coconut water instead.
options.feedback: India's food guide warns that people with some heart or kidney problems should avoid coconut water.

items.stem: After hours in the heat, which sign calls for urgent help, not just a drink?

options.text: Confusion, or dizziness that will not pass.
options.feedback: If you are confused or dizzy and it does not pass, the body may be badly short of water. Get help fast.
Mild thirst is a cue to drink. It is not by itself a red flag.
Pale yellow pee is the aim. It shows the body has enough fluid.

concepts.title: Sleep and recovery
concepts.hook: Sleep is active: the brain stores the day's learning while the body carries out repair.
concepts.rule: Adults need seven or more hours of sleep, which stores learning and repairs the body. Sleep runs in cycles of about 90 minutes, with deep sleep early. A fixed wake time and a dark room help.

claims.text: CDC recommends seven or more hours of sleep for adults aged 18–60.
Early in the night, the body puts deep sleep first to recover. Towards morning, deep sleep gets shorter and REM sleep gets longer.
One full sleep cycle takes about 80 to 100 minutes, and most people go through four to six cycles a night. Most vivid dreams happen in REM sleep.
Habits that help sleep include the same bed and wake time each day, a quiet, cool and dark bedroom, devices off at least 30 minutes before bed, and no caffeine late in the day.
Caffeine can take 8 hours or more to wear off fully.
Sleep helps with learning and forming long-term memories, deep sleep boosts the repair of cells and tissues, and cutting sleep by even one hour can make it hard to focus.

concepts.title: Reading a food label
concepts.hook: Two packs can use different serving sizes. The per-100-g line puts them on the same base so you can compare them.
concepts.rule: Compare like foods on their per-100-g or per-100-ml lines. Ingredients run from most to least. Front-of-pack marketing claims like 'real fruit' can mislead, so the back label tells more.

claims.text: Nutrition values are given per 100 g or 100 ml, and may also be given per serving, whose size each brand sets.
Packed food lists its ingredients in order, with the largest amount first.
India's food guide says front-of-pack claims can mislead. A 'real fruit' product may hold 10% fruit or less. A 'sugar free' food may carry sweeteners like maltitol, fat or white flour.
If a pack holds two servings of 100 kcal each, eating the whole pack gives 200 kcal.
India's food guide says 'all natural' is often used loosely, so the ingredients on the back should be read to check the claim.

items.stem: A friend says a snack is light because the label shows 'only 80 kcal per serving'. What is missing?

options.text: How many servings the pack holds.
options.feedback: If the pack holds three servings, eating it all gives 240 kcal, not 80.
The figure is per serving, and a pack often holds more than one.

options.text: The weight of the empty wrapper.
options.feedback: The wrapper tells you nothing. The number of servings changes the total.

items.stem: Reading the label, a 40 g packet of namkeen has 1.5 g of salt per 100 g. Estimate the salt in the whole packet.

options.feedback: 40 g is 0.4 of 100 g, so 1.5 g times 0.4 is about 0.6 g.
That is the figure for 100 g. The packet holds only 40 g.
The decimal slipped. A packet smaller than 100 g holds less than 1.5 g, about 0.6 g.

items.stem: Namkeen A lists salt third; namkeen B lists it fifth. Yet B has more salt per 100 g. How can that be?

options.text: List order ranks items inside one pack, not across packs.
options.feedback: Order shows what is biggest within a pack. To compare two packs, use the per 100 g line.

options.text: The label on B has to be wrong.
options.feedback: Both labels can be right. Order ranks items within one pack, not between packs.

options.text: Fifth place means less salt in every case.
options.feedback: Fifth place only ranks salt against B's other items. Per 100 g compares packs.

items.stem: A trail mix holds 40% oats, 25% sugar, 20% nuts and 15% raisins. Put them in label order.

options.feedback: At 40%, oats are the largest part, so they lead the list.
At 25%, sugar is the second largest part.
At 20%, nuts come after sugar in the list.
At 15%, raisins are the smallest part, so they come last.

items.stem: At the school canteen, a chips pack shouts 'all natural' in big letters. What is the sensible next step?

options.text: Read the ingredients on the back.
options.feedback: 'Natural' is often used loosely to sell, so the back label shows what is really inside.

options.text: Trust it, since 'natural' is a strict rule.

options.text: Pick it over a pack with no claims.

options.feedback: Per 100 g the two are nearly the same, because sugar-free snacks can carry fat and flour.

steps.title: Compare on the per 100 g line

hook.stem: Two biscuit packs list sugar per serving, but their servings differ. What is the fair way to compare?

options.feedback: Right. Per 100 g puts both packs on the same base.
Pack size does not make a fair test. The per 100 g line does.

options.text: Go with the brand you have heard of.
options.feedback: A familiar name tells you nothing about sugar. Compare per 100 g.

steps.teach: Each brand picks its own serving size, so per-serving numbers cannot be compared fairly. The per 100 g or 100 ml line puts every pack on the same base.

example.ask: Tap the fair line to compare.
parts: Pack A says 6 g sugar per 20 g serving,
Pack B says 9 g per 50 g serving,
but per 100 g, A has 30 g and B has 18 g.
example.spot: but per 100 g, A has 30 g and B has 18 g.
example.feedback: On the same 100 g base, Pack A has far more sugar, even though its serving shows less.

guided.stem: Why is a per-serving number hard to compare across brands?
guided.hint: Ask who decides the portion size.

options.text: Each brand sets its own serving.
options.feedback: Right. One brand’s serving may be far bigger or smaller than another’s, and a pack may hold several servings.
Servings vary from pack to pack. The per 100 g line is the fixed one.

options.text: The numbers are printed too small.
options.feedback: Print size is not the trouble. Serving sizes differ between brands.

steps.takeaway: Compare packs on the per 100 g or per 100 ml line.

steps.title: Ingredients run from most to least

hook.stem: A list reads: sugar, wheat flour, palm oil, cocoa. What is there most of?

options.feedback: Right. The first ingredient is the one with the largest amount.
Cocoa comes last, so there is the least of it.

options.text: You can't tell from a list.
options.feedback: You can. Ingredients run from the most to the least.

steps.teach: Ingredients are listed by amount, the most first, so the first few tell you what the food mostly is. Sugar near the top means a lot of sugar.

example.ask: Tap the main ingredient.
parts: The muesli pack lists sugar first,
then oats and nuts,
with dried fruit near the end.
example.spot: The muesli pack lists sugar first,

guided.stem: A chips pack lists potato, oil, salt. Which is there least of?
guided.hint: Look at the end of the list.

options.feedback: Yes. Salt comes last, so there is the least of it of the three.
Potato comes first, so there is the most of it.
Oil is in the middle. Salt, at the end, is the smallest amount.

steps.takeaway: The first ingredient is the one there is most of.

steps.title: Front claims sell; the back tells

hook.stem: A drink pack says 'made with real fruit'. How much fruit can that mean?

options.feedback: Right. India's food guide says a 'real fruit' claim can sit on a drink with 10% fruit or less.
The rule is far looser. The claim can cover 10% fruit or less.

options.text: Pure fruit with no water added.
options.feedback: It need not be pure. The claim can cover 10% fruit or less.

options.text: It has no sweetener in it.

concepts.title: Fad diet claims
concepts.hook: A juice 'detox' promises 5 kg off in a week. Slow loss of about half a kilo a week is safer, and no single food covers every need.
concepts.rule: A varied diet supplies different nutrients, and no one food covers every need. Detox diets lack strong proof. For people who need to lose weight, safe loss is slow, about half a kilo a week.

claims.text: ICMR-NIN says to eat from many food groups. No one food gives all the key nutrients.
WHO gives a guide of at least 400 g of fruit and vegetables a day for everyone older than 10.
NCCIH finds no strong research that detox diets help weight loss; juice and detox diets cause early loss because people eat few calories, and the weight tends to return with normal eating.
India's food guide says weight loss should be slow. About half a kilogram a week is called safe. Rapid weight-loss plans and diet drugs should be avoided.
In India's food guide plate, vegetables, fruits, greens, roots and tubers make up about half the plate.
Fasting can cause headaches, fainting, weakness and dehydration. Diets that cut calories hard rarely give lasting loss and may miss some nutrients.

items.stem: Unlike a fad diet that drops vegetables, your family of four plans the day's shopping with at least 400 g of fruit and vegetables each. Estimate the total.

options.feedback: Four people at 400 g each need 1,600 g, which is 1.6 kg of fruit and vegetables.
That is one person's share. Four people need four times as much, about 1.6 kg.
The decimal slipped. Four times 400 g is 1,600 g, or 1.6 kg.

items.stem: A friend says milk is a complete food, so an adult could live on milk alone. What is not quite right?

options.text: No single food, milk included, has every nutrient.
options.feedback: Milk is rich in many nutrients, but India's food guide notes it is not a source of iron. A mix of groups is needed.
Milk misses some nutrients, such as iron. No single food covers every need.

options.text: Milk is fine, but just for children.
options.feedback: Age is not the point. No single food, milk included, covers every nutrient.

items.stem: Two weeks after her juice cleanse, Tara weighs what she did before. Her friend says the juice was too weak. What explains it better?

options.text: The early drop came from eating little, so it returned.
options.feedback: Detox loss comes from eating few calories, and it tends to come back once normal meals start.

options.text: She chose the wrong brand of juice.
options.feedback: No juice brand fixes this. The early drop came from eating little, so it returned.

options.text: Her body stored the toxins again.
options.feedback: There is no strong research on detox clearing toxins. The drop came from eating little.

items.stem: During exam week, Kunal plans two no-food 'cleanse' days to feel light. What risk does he take?

options.feedback: Going without food for days can cause headaches, weakness, fainting and dehydration.
No-food days tend to bring headaches and weakness, which make study harder, not easier.

options.text: No risk, if he drinks tea.
options.feedback: Tea does not remove the risk. No-food days can cause headaches, weakness and fainting.

items.stem: A college friend shares a reel: one glass of jeera water each morning melts belly fat overnight. What are the red flags?

options.text: One drink, and an overnight result.
options.feedback: No single food does everything, and loss that fast is far beyond the slow, safe pace.

options.text: None, if the reel has many views.
options.feedback: Views do not make a claim true. One magic drink and an overnight result are both red flags.

options.text: The drink costs too little to work.
options.feedback: Price is not the clue. One magic drink and an overnight result are the red flags.

options.text: Yes, everyone should lose that much each week.
options.feedback: The pace is for people who need to lose weight, not a goal for everyone.
Season does not matter. The pace is meant for people who need to lose weight.

steps.title: Detox plans lack proof

options.feedback: Right. Early loss on a detox usually returns once normal eating starts.
The early drop usually returns once normal meals start again.

options.text: It cleans the body of toxins for good.
options.feedback: There is no strong research that detox plans clear toxins or help weight loss.

options.feedback: Loss should be gradual, about half a kilo a week, for people who need to lose weight.
